summary:
At most one option can have more than half the votes. Boyer–Moore voting finds the only option that
*could* (pairs of different votes cancel, and a true majority survives), then one counting pass checks
whether it really does. O(n) time, O(1) space.

question.md:
Return the option that received **strictly more than half** of the votes, or −1 if none did.

- **"More than half" is strict:** in 4 votes, 2 isn't enough; you need 3. `[1, 2, 1, 2]` gives −1.
- **There may be no winner.** This is the difference from a problem that *promises* a majority: any
  shortcut that guesses a winner must then **verify** it.
- **At most one winner exists**: two options each with more than half would need more than n votes.
- **Size:** up to 10⁵ votes, option ids up to 10⁹ (so they can't index an array). The goal is O(1)
  extra space.

think.md:
Take `[4, 9, 4, 4, 2, 4, 9]`: option 4 has 4 of 7 votes, a winner. And `[6, 1, 6, 2, 6, 3]`: option 6 has 3
of 6, exactly half, so no winner.

Imagine pairing up votes for **different** options and throwing each pair away. A winner has more
votes than all the others combined, so it can't be paired off completely; something of it always
survives. But the reverse fails: in `[6, 1, 6, 2, 6, 3]` the cancelling still ends with 6 as the
survivor, even though 6 has only half the votes, not more.

think.caption: 6 survives the cancelling, yet 3 of 6 votes is not more than half. A survivor is only a candidate.

think.md:
So the plan has two steps: **find the candidate** cheaply by cancelling, then **count** it once to see
whether it truly passes n/2.

approaches.title: Count each option by scanning

idea.md: For each vote, count how many votes share its option. The first option whose count is more than n/2 wins; if none is, return −1.

build: For each vote `x`, count the votes equal to `x` with a scan.

lines.text: Try each vote's option as the possible winner.
Count its votes with a full scan. `c × 2 > n` is "more than half" without the rounding of `n / 2`.

steps.text: [4, 9, 4, 4, 2, 4, 9]: option 4 has 4 of 7 votes, more than half.
[6, 1, 6, 2, 6, 3]: every option counted; the most any has is 3 of 6, not more than half.

walk.title: Count each vote's option with a full scan until one has more than half.

limits.md: The same option is recounted for every one of its votes. Counting all options in one pass removes the repetition, at the cost of memory.

approaches.title: Count in a hash map

idea.md: One pass counts every option in a hash map; return the option whose count passes n/2 (stop as soon as one does), else −1.

build: For each vote, increment its count; if `count × 2 > n`, return it.

lines.text: C has no hash map: a slot holds an option, its count and an in-use flag; `slotOf` scrambles an option into a starting slot.

notes.c: A power-of-two table at least 2n big; `winner` stays −1 until an option passes half (option ids are ≥ 0, so −1 can't be confused with one).

lines.text: Add this vote to its option's count.

notes.c: Probe forward from the option's slot to its entry or an empty slot, and claim it.

lines.text: The moment a count passes half, that option has won; nothing later can change it.

complexity.md: **Time O(n)** on average. **Space O(n)** for the counts.

walk.title: Count every option in a hash map; check whether the largest count passes n/2.

limits.md: It keeps a count for every option, although at most one can win. Voting needs only one candidate and one counter; the price is a second pass to verify.

approaches.title: Boyer–Moore vote, then verify

idea.md:
**Pass 1 (find a candidate):** keep `candidate` and `count`. When `count` is 0 the current vote
becomes the candidate; a matching vote adds 1, a different vote subtracts 1. Each subtraction
discards one candidate vote together with one different vote. A real winner has more votes than
everyone else together, so it can never be fully discarded: if a winner exists, it is the final
candidate.

**Pass 2 (verify):** the candidate might not be a winner (when there is none, the survivor is
arbitrary). Count its votes and return it only if the count passes n/2.

build: For each vote: if `count == 0`, adopt it; then `count += 1` if it equals the candidate, else `count −= 1`.
Count the candidate's votes in a second pass.

lines.text: No candidate yet; a count of 0 means the next vote takes over.
The cancelling pass: matching votes strengthen the candidate, different ones cancel one of its votes.

notes.cpp: The local `count` shadows `std::count`, which is why the verify step names `std::count` in full.

lines.text: The survivor is only the *possible* winner. Count its real votes.
It wins only with strictly more than half.

steps.text: Check: 4 has 4 of 7 votes → more than half, it wins.
Check: 6 has 3 of 6 votes → not more than half, so −1.

walk.title: Voting finds the only possible winner; a second pass checks it really has more than half.

takeaways.md:
- Boyer–Moore voting returns the majority **if one exists**. When it might not, always verify with a
  second count.
- "More than half" in integer code: `count * 2 > n`, avoiding `n / 2` rounding mistakes.
- Compare with **Majority Reading**, where the majority is guaranteed and the verify pass can be dropped.
